Personally I have quite a few games which have impacted my early gaming life.

Total annihilation and the original Command and Conquer cemented my love of RTS games, even if I am awful at them. The rush of building that huge army and rushing into the enemy base was insane and made me feel very powerful, the work I put early in the game paid off.

Medal and Honour and Battlefield 1942 made me realise that theres not much which beats the rush of a fast paced arcade style online first person shooter, running in with your team, seeing your friends dying to your left and right and getting headshots to avenge them. my K98 or M1 gerand was my best friend.

I'm also going to mention that Total Annihilation and Bf1942 also made me realise just how awesome the modding community is. I added new races and textures and units to Total annihilation, there was even a complete ACDC themed remake of the game. As far bf192, the modern combat mod was great but nothing beat the star wars mod, complete with sound effects from vacuum cleaners, and the canyon maps perfect for X wing racing through hairpin canyon turns with lasers flying past your ship.

Rollercoaster Tycoon, Theme park, theme hospital and Sim city (As well as Sim Ant!) made me realise building from scratch, planning and juggling resources in strategic building games was so fun, maybe it hit some of the same triggers as RTS games for me, but these were definitely fond memories.

Pokemon blue/red on the gameboy, I spent easily 1000 hours on this game, I had countless pokemon at level 100. This game along with Final Fantasy 8 made me realise I had a love for RPGs that is still alive and strong to this day.

I was also into some pretty dodgy free to play MMORPGs, most notably for me was Conquer Online, it was weird and pay to win, but I loved it, I loved my guild which I became leader of, I spent years of my life on this game with people I considered amazing friends. Most days I wouldn't even play, I'd just log on to chat. I knew almost every person on my server, it was a big family.

Total Annihilation is awesome!! I still play it every so often! TA Spring was really cool too, spent lots of time playing multiplayer. It even had first person control of units, which I think is incredibly creative and also really, really pointless when playing competitively.

It's not the start of my gaming career, but I'd have to say Super Smash Bros. for the Nintendo 64 had the biggest impact. My brother and I used to fight all of the time. We were both good at video games and would get way too competitive to the point of arguments and rage quits (we were young). Super Smash Bros. was the game where we discovered playing together in a team instead of constantly pitting ourselves against one another. To our surprise we liked this a lot more. Now instead of being frustrated at his success, I welcomed it. I had spent enough time predicting his moves in competitive play that it was second nature to rely on him in cooperative play. We've been playing co-op and team games ever since, and I've found that we're often the only team in the room that doesn't communicate at all because we don't really need to. I know how he reacts to things and he knows me as well. He lives in another state now, but we still get together at least once a week to play co-op or pit ourselves against the competition in team vs team matchups. Super Smash Bros. wasn't the first game we played together, but it's probably the point where we stopped being adversaries and started being brothers.

When I finally got that game (like the January after it came out) I was fucking addicted to it. Everyday after practice until I went to bed I'd be playing that. I was never particularly good at it, but I liked playing the game even though my mom hated it.

Fast forward to mid February. My parents were in the early stages of a divorce and this point and my dad had already moved out. I come home from school and sit right on the couch and start playing. Once dinner is ready, I eat and go back to playing. Around 8:30 that night I walk upstairs to get something from my room and I hear my mom crying in her room. I walk into the room, and part way though asking whats wrong it hits me- its her fucking birthday.

I had gotten so sucked into that piece of shit game that I forgot about my own mothers birthday. I didn't get a gift or even wish her a happy birthday at all that day.

That night was a massive wakeup call for me. I still game, probably more than I should, but I never make a game the only thing on my mind. I'm never turning into the piece of shit I was at that time again.

So yeah. MW2 changed my life. Fucking weird thinking about it like that.

Everybody always cites X-Wing or Wing Commander, but for me it was FreeSpace all the way. At the time, I was pretty out of my depth with the complicated controls, but the epic storyline was absolutely engrossing to my young self.
My Dad would let me sit on his lap while he played, and I would "co-pilot" during missions, doing things like managing the more fiddly parts of the targeting systems (there was a surprising amount of nuance in there), managing power distribution to the ships sub-systems (engines/weapons/shields) and communicating with the wingmen and Command.

In addition to the gameplay, I still hold it up as one of the best examples of how to blend a fairly rich story into an action based game.

If you'll allow me to digress a bit;

The game's main menu was a full-screen animated render of the interior of an enormous aircraft-carrier styled spaceship called the Galatea (which, not coincidentally, is the hostname of my current laptop), and different parts of the menu would be activated by clicking on doors leading to different parts of the ship. Hovering over doors would cause them to slide open, giving a peek at the rooms behind them, and you could see people and machinery moving around in the background.

At various points during the campaign, things would happen to the Galatea that would be reflected in the menu. After a major battle the doors might get stuck sometimes, or you would see more alarm lights and less crewmen, etc. Spoilers for a ~20 year old game:

The campaign was fairly linear, but did a really good job of making you feel like a small part of a living world. In one mission you might encounter a new enemy and be completely outclassed, desperately hoping Command would give the order to fall back; later you would get a detailed briefing on where your battlegroup was being re-positioned to bypass the new threat; sometime after that, you would get a special mission to sneak past the enemy lines and capture tech samples; later still, your researchers would finally figure out the principles, and start producing (sometimes buggy) prototypes that you would get to test.

/end digression

ANYWAY: I still love that game, and FreeSpace I/II pretty much set the gold standard for what I want out of science-fiction action games.

FreeSpace is also directly responsible for hooking me on open-source software, since the FS2 engine source code was released sometime not long after the game was published. That engine continues to be developed (latest release was in April of this year), and between rendering upgrades and an amazing community of modders, still gives modern space sims a pretty good run for their money (not that there were that many modern space sims, at least until pretty recently).
